newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech output shrinks as c.bank measures bite.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech output shrinks as c.bank measures bite.

text.p: Czech industrial and construction output posted their second consecutive monthly contraction in February as the central bank's restrictive monetary policy continues to stifle growth.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said on Wednesday that real industrial production shrank 5.8 percent year-on-year in February, while construction output also slumped, falling a real 1.6 percent over the same month of the previous year.

It was the second time in as many months that both have fallen, and analysts said the figures could be attributed mainly to the tight monetary policy which has cooled the economy in an attempt to choke inflation.
"The figures are not particularly surprising. It's obviously a result of the tight money policy the central bank has put in place," said Jonathan Garner of Robert Fleming Securities.

"Unfortunately it's painful and it takes time for that to begin to affect wage growth and the trade balance which remain the two main problems. But there are signs it is working in terms of M2 money and the inflation rate," he added.
The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of demand-led growth as industry imported technology and a sharp rise in wages provoked a consumer boom.

Last summer, the central bank raised its key discount rate by one percentage point to 10.5 percent, and implemented a series of measures to slow a rapidly-growing money supply and ease inflationary pressures.

The moves appear to be working, with growth in M2 money supply, which measures currency, demand deposits, time and savings deposits, and foreign currency deposits, easing to 7.8 percent in December from 20.2 percent in the same month of 1995.
On Tuesday the CSU said inflation fell to an all-time low of 6.8 percent year-on-year in March.

In Thursday's report, the CSU said that wage growth slowed in February to a nominal 11.4 percent, down from 14.4 percent the previous month. But analysts said it was too soon to see a real trend in the figures.

"It's starting to affect the real economy but it is going to take time for that to seep through to wage growth," said one local analyst. "That is why we are seeing the central bank constantly stating it will not back off higher rates."

The government has said it will introduce a package of measures to help the economy on April 16. Though it has not mentioned specific measures, local media have reported an import surcharge and public sector wage limits as solutions.

Ironically, while most of Europe continues to battle high unemployment, analysts said they were disappointed with data released on Wednesday that showed the jobless rate dropped to 3.9 percent in March from February's 4.1 percent. Low unemployment encourages wage growth as employers compete for workers.

"We were a little disappointed with the unemployment figure yesterday which was a little unexpected. But that is the only figure this week that has not been in line with our expectations," said Lubos Kacmarik of Creditanstalt.
"The wage growth figure is good...it comes close to the central bank's magic number of 10 percent," he said.
Analysts said the market is now focused on January M2 money supply figures, expected to be released on Thursday, which may prove to be the final data that persuades the central bank to move on rates.

A flood of about 35 billion crowns ($1.2 billion) worth of crown-denominated Eurobonds was issued that month. The central bank has been working furiously to keep the funds that came into the Czech Republic in the form of swaps to back the paper out of the money supply.
"There is a threat to M2 in how much of the Eurobond money came into the economy. We will see if the central bank has been successful in sterilising," Kacmarik said.
